questions.question: Q1. In the simulation, you started at 640×480 resolution (Z = 1 m) and saw a dense cloud with 2-3 mm spacing. When you dropped the resolution to 320×240, what happened to the point count and spacing?

answers.a: Point count got cut in half, and spacing stayed the same
answers.b: Point count plummeted to a quarter (76,800), and spacing doubled to 4-6 mm
answers.c: Point count stayed exactly the same, but the points got closer together
answers.d: Point count actually went up because lower resolution captures more detail

explanations.a: Not quite! You halved the width AND the height, which means the total area (and point count) shrank by a factor of 4, not 2. And since there are fewer points covering the same area, spacing has to increase.
explanations.b: Nailed it! Because N_total = width × height, dropping both dimensions in half reduces your total points by a factor of 4 (from 307k to ~77k). And since you have way fewer pixels covering the same physical space, the gap between each point doubles. You probably saw some pretty big holes in your 3D view!
explanations.c: Nope. If you take fewer samples (lower resolution) over the same area, the points physically have to spread out.
explanations.d: Backwards! Lower resolution means fewer pixels, which directly translates to fewer 3D points.

questions.question: Q2. You added a chunky σ = 30 mm noise to a flat wall at Z = 2 m, making it look all wavy. Then you dialed it down to σ = 2 mm. What changed visually, and why?

answers.a: Nothing changed; noise only affects the color of the points
answers.b: The wavy bumps vanished and the wall looked flat again, because each point had a much smaller random error in its depth
answers.c: The point cloud got way denser because low noise generates more valid points
answers.d: The wall appeared to jump closer to the camera

explanations.a: Incorrect. Noise messes directly with the Z (depth) coordinate, which physically moves the point in 3D space. It's structural, not just cosmetic.
explanations.b: Exactly! With σ = 30 mm, your points were randomly jumping forward and backward by large amounts, creating a wavy mess. Dropping σ to 2 mm meant the random jitter was tiny, so the points snapped back into a tight, nearly perfect flat plane. It’s a perfect visual of the Z_measured = Z_true + N(0, σ²) formula in action!
explanations.c: Nope. Noise affects where the points are placed, not how many points are created. That's determined by your resolution.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Our noise model is centered at zero, meaning it randomly scatters points forward AND backward. It doesn't systematically pull the whole wall forward.

questions.question: Q3. You scanned a cube using a focal length of 700 px, but the real calibrated value was 770 px. How did this 10% error mess with your point cloud's shape?

answers.a: It didn't—focal length errors don't affect geometry
answers.b: The cube looked about 10% wider and taller because dividing by a smaller focal length artificially inflates the X and Y coordinates
answers.c: The cube stayed the same size because the math naturally cancels out the error

explanations.a: Incorrect. Focal length is a core part of the back-projection formula. If it's wrong, your entire 3D geometry is warped.
explanations.b: Spot on! In our formula X = (u-cx) × Z / fx, fx is at the bottom of the fraction. If you use 700 instead of the true 770, you're dividing by a smaller number, which makes your resulting X and Y coordinates roughly 10% bigger. Your cube got stretched out like a balloon!
explanations.c: Nope. There's no magical cancellation here. An error in fx creates a direct, uncorrected error in your final 3D shape.
explanations.d: Backwards! Because fx is in the denominator, using a smaller number makes your final coordinates larger, not smaller.

questions.question: Q4. You scanned an object at 2 meters, then backed it up to 4 meters. The bounding box volume quadrupled, but the point density plummeted. What's the takeaway here?

answers.a: It's a bug in the simulation physics engine
answers.b: As distance grows, your camera's field of view covers a larger physical area, forcing the same amount of pixels to stretch over a wider space
answers.d: Bounding boxes and point density have absolutely no mathematical connection

explanations.a: Not a bug at all! This is exactly how real-world optics and depth sensors behave.
explanations.b: You got it! Your camera has a fixed number of pixels. As you move further away, its cone of vision expands to cover a massive chunk of the room (huge bounding box). But since you still only have, say, 300,000 points, they have to spread out way thinner to cover that space. Massive area + fixed point count = terrible density.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The exact opposite happens. Spreading your points over a larger distant area ruins your density.
explanations.d: Nope. They are two sides of the same coin, directly linked by how the camera's field of view expands with distance.

questions.question: Q5. You noticed some annoying 'flying pixels' floating between a foreground box and the background wall. What's the best way to get rid of them at the source?

answers.a: Crank up the camera resolution to max
answers.b: Improve the sensor's edge-handling algorithms so it doesn't get confused at sharp depth drops
answers.c: Just move the camera further back
answers.d: Change the color palette to hide them

explanations.a: Nope. More resolution just means you might get even MORE flying pixels, because the sensor will still get confused right at the edge.
explanations.b: Exactly! Flying pixels happen because the sensor literally panics when a single pixel straddles a close object and a far wall, blending the depths. The true fix is better sensor logic (or software filters) that recognize this boundary and throw away the confused data.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The physical edge and depth drop still exist even if you step back.
explanations.d: That's just sweeping the dirt under the rug! The bad geometry is still there, even if you paint it black.

questions.question: Q6. You ran two tests at 3 meters. Run A used a focal length of 350 px, and Run B used 1400 px. How did the field of view and point cloud spread differ between them?

answers.a: They looked exactly the same; focal length doesn't change the field of view
answers.b: Run A (350 px) acted like a wide-angle lens, capturing a huge wide area. Run B (1400 px) acted like a zoomed-in telephoto lens, capturing a tiny, dense patch of the scene
answers.c: Run B had the wider field of view because a bigger number means more area
answers.d: Run B generated 4 times as many points as Run A

explanations.a: Incorrect. Focal length is the absolute key to determining how wide or narrow your camera's vision is.
explanations.b: Perfect! A small focal length (350 px) means a massive, wide field of view—so your point cloud stretches out far and wide. A huge focal length (1400 px) is highly zoomed in, so your point cloud is just a tight, compact square capturing a tiny sliver of the room.
explanations.c: Backwards! In optics, a larger focal length means a narrower, more zoomed-in field of view.
explanations.d: Nope. Both runs had the same resolution, so they produced the exact same number of points. Run B's points were just squeezed into a smaller physical area.

questions.question: Q7. You scanned a flat plane with 4 mm noise, getting an RMSE of about 4 mm. If you crank the noise up to 8 mm, what happens to the RMSE, and what does this prove?

answers.a: RMSE shoots up to 16 mm, proving that error scales quadratically
answers.b: RMSE doubles to 8 mm, proving that in this direct noise model, the error scales perfectly linearly with the noise parameter
answers.d: RMSE drops to 2 mm because the noise cancels itself out

explanations.a: Incorrect. You're thinking of the stereo disparity formula from Experiment 1, which has a squared term. This back-projection noise model is much simpler.
explanations.b: Exactly! Because we literally just add the noise directly to the depth (Z_measured = Z_true + N(0, σ²)), the resulting error (RMSE) is basically identical to the noise standard deviation (σ). If you double the noise setting, you perfectly double your final error. It's a clean, linear relationship.
explanations.c: Nope! If you feed the system more noise, the resulting cloud gets messier and the RMSE definitely goes up.
explanations.d: Incorrect. More noise means a rougher surface and a higher error. It doesn't magically fix itself.

questions.question: Q8. You scanned a scene with a close object (0.5 m) and a far wall (8 m) using a fixed 5 mm noise. How did the visual quality compare between the two, and why?

answers.a: They looked equally noisy because 5 mm of noise is 5 mm of noise
answers.b: The close object looked super clean, but the far wall looked like a jagged mess. Because points are spread so far apart at 8m, that 5 mm jitter is way more obvious and destructive
answers.c: The far wall looked smoother because noise naturally fades away over distance
answers.d: The simulation crashed because it can't handle two depths at once

explanations.a: Incorrect. While the math applies the same 5 mm of jitter, the visual impact is totally different depending on how tightly packed the points are.
explanations.b: Spot on! Up close (0.5 m), your points are packed so incredibly tight that a tiny 5 mm wobble barely registers—the surface looks solid. But way out at 8 m, the points are already hugely spaced out. Adding a 5 mm wobble to a sparse, dotty grid turns it into a chaotic, jagged mess. Distance ruins point density, which makes noise look much worse!
explanations.c: Nope! Real sensors actually get noisier at a distance. But even with a fixed noise level, the sparse density far away makes it look worse, not better.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Real scenes (and our simulation) have depth variations everywhere.

questions.question: Q9. You ran a perfect simulation with zero noise. Then you intentionally added a +5 px error to the principal point (cx). What happened, and how is this different from random sensor noise?

answers.a: Nothing happened; cx only affects the camera's colors
answers.b: The whole point cloud slid sideways predictably. Unlike random noise (which averages out over time), this is a systematic bias that permanently warps every scan exactly the same way
answers.c: The points scattered everywhere, looking exactly like random noise
answers.d: The simulation locked up because cx cannot be changed

explanations.a: Incorrect. cx is literally the center point of our geometry math. If it's wrong, everything shifts.
explanations.b: Nailed it! A wrong cx value shifts every single X coordinate in the exact same direction by a predictable amount. It takes your perfect point cloud and physically slides it sideways. This is called systematic error—and it's nasty because you can't fix it by just taking 100 scans and averaging them out. Random noise can be averaged; bad calibration is forever (until you recalibrate)!
explanations.c: Nope! Random noise looks like rough sandpaper. A calibration error looks perfectly smooth, just sitting in the completely wrong location.
explanations.d: Incorrect. We let you break it on purpose so you can see why calibration is so crucial!

questions.question: Q10. You noticed flying pixels around the edge of a cube at 640×480 resolution. If you bump the resolution up to 1280×960, what happens to those edge artifacts?

answers.a: They completely vanish because 4K cameras don't have this problem
answers.b: You might actually see MORE of them in total, but they stay tightly hugged to the edge. The core physical problem of the sensor getting confused at a cliff edge hasn't gone away
answers.c: Resolution has absolutely nothing to do with it

explanations.a: Incorrect. Even an ultra-HD sensor will get confused when a single pixel is half-on a close box and half-on a far wall.
explanations.b: Correct! Because you quadrupled the pixel count, you have way more pixels hanging out near the danger zone (the edge). So you might get a higher raw count of flying pixels. But they don't spread out further—they still hug the physical boundary. Resolution just gives you a higher-definition picture of the same fundamental sensor glitch. You need smart filtering software, not just more megapixels, to fix it.
explanations.c: Incorrect. More resolution means more edge-sampling, which definitely changes how the artifacts appear numerically, even if it doesn't cure the disease.
explanations.d: Nope. It's a universal problem for depth cameras, regardless of their resolution setting.
